objectives: Build answers from a pass from the left and a pass from the right.
Normalize remainders so they're never negative in any language.
Recognize that two equal running remainders mean the values between them add up to a multiple.

sections.heading: Intuition: running state from both sides, and around a clock
paragraphs: Day 20's prefix sums summarize everything to the left of a position. Some problems also need everything to the right. A second pass from the right end builds that, and then each position can combine its left and right summaries.

Remainders behave like a clock. On a 12-hour clock, moving forward 5 and then back 17 lands where you started, because the moves add up to -12. If a running clock position ever repeats, the moves between the two visits add up to a whole number of laps: a multiple of 12.

callout.text: Two running totals with the same remainder mod m mean the values between them add up to a multiple of m.

diagram.description: A clock at 0 moves +5 to 5, then -3 to 2, then +10 back to 0. The three moves add up to 12.

sections.heading: Baseline: check every range
paragraphs: Checking every range's sum for divisibility is O(n²) even with prefix sums. Remembering remainders you've already seen turns "does some earlier position match?" into one map lookup.

sections.heading: Worked example: find a run of moves that makes a full lap
paragraphs: A clock starts at 0 and applies shifts one at a time. Keep a set of every hour it has shown, starting with 0. After each shift, compute the new hour. If it's already in the set, the shifts since the clock last showed that hour add up to a multiple of 12.
Computing the hour needs care with negative shifts. In Python, -5 % 12 is 7. In C++, Java, and Go, it's -5. Writing ((hour + shift) % m + m) % m gives the same, non-negative answer in every language.

callout.text: Recording hour 0 before any step matters. Without it, a run of shifts starting at the very first one could never be found.

sections.heading: Complexity and cautions
paragraphs: The clock scan is O(n) time with at most m remembered remainders. Two passes, one from each side, are O(n) time and O(n) memory, or O(1) extra if you build the answer in the output array.
Normalize remainders before using them as keys: -5 and 7 are the same position on a 12-hour clock, but they're different map keys.

sections.heading: Before you finish
paragraphs: Try to answer each question before opening it.

checks.prompt: On a 12-hour clock, the positions after some shifts are 0, 5, 2, 0. What do the three shifts add up to, mod 12?
checks.answer: 0. The clock returned to where it was, so the shifts form whole laps: a multiple of 12.

checks.prompt: What is (-5 % 12 + 12) % 12, and why write it that way?
checks.answer: 7. It's non-negative in every language, even where -5 % 12 is -5.

checks.prompt: Why record hour 0 before the first step?
checks.answer: So a run that starts with the very first shift can be detected when the clock returns to 0.
